squalid

SKWAH-lid · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Squalid is extremely dirty, neglected, and unpleasant, especially as a result of poverty.

The novel's opening chapter describes a squalid tenement building in vivid, uncomfortable detail -- crumbling plaster, rats in the walls, and a single broken faucet shared by twelve families.

Example

Investigators were shocked by the squalid state of the warehouse where the animals had been kept, with no clean water and waste piled knee-deep in every cage.

Squalid describes conditions that are extremely dirty and neglected, usually as a result of poverty or severe mistreatment -- here, filthy, waste-filled cages.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

filthy: Filthy means extremely dirty and nothing more — grease, dust, or grime in shocking amounts, with no story behind it. Squalid goes further: the dirt comes with neglect, decay, and usually poverty, so a squalid place feels wretched, not just unwashed. A kitchen floor can be filthy; a slum is squalid.

sordid: Sordid adds moral disgrace to the dirt: a sordid affair or sordid motives are shameful, not merely grubby. Squalid stays physical — it describes the actual state of rooms, buildings, and living conditions. A squalid apartment offends the eyes; a sordid scheme offends the conscience.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

pristine: spotlessly clean, as if new

immaculate: perfectly clean and tidy, without a single flaw

Where it sits · how deep the filth and decay go — grimy → squalid → fetid

grimy vs. squalid: Something grimy is simply covered in dirt or grime, without squalid's fuller sense of poverty-driven neglect and decay.

fetid vs. squalid: Something fetid combines squalid dirtiness with an overpowering stench, an even more visceral, intense image than squalid alone.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — squal-

root — squal-: to be dirty, filthy, or scaly (Latin squalere)

suffix — -id

suffix — -id: characterized by, full of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Squalid comes from Latin squalere ('to be filthy or covered in scaly grime') plus the adjective suffix -id ('characterized by'). This is the very same root behind the noun squalor, which you already learned earlier in this course -- squalid conditions are, quite literally, conditions marked by squalor.

Use the root in a new word: squalor

Use the root in a new word: squalor: You already learned this word: squalor is the noun form, describing the filthy, neglected condition itself -- families were forced to live in squalor for years after the flood.
